2.1.3. Extrema-segmented entropy (ExSEnt)

ExSEnt recodes the signal into sequences of segment durations and amplitudes defined by its local extrema, then applies SampEn to each. It thus emphasizes the temporal and morphological organization of the waveform instead of sample-by-sample similarity, which should make it less sensitive to slow drifts and amplitude scaling [36]. ExSEnt is computed per EEG channel by first transforming the time series into sequences defined by extrema-based segmentation and then calculating SampEn. Given a time series x(t), extrema are identified at sign changes of the first difference Δx(t) = x(t+1) -x(t) at which the change in slope, |Δx(t) -Δx(t-1)|, exceeds a robust threshold, θ = λ ⋅ IQR ( Δx ) (10) where λ controls the sensitivity of extrema detection (λ = 0.001 by default in ASCENT, which is more permissive than the λ = 0.01 used by Kamali et al. [36]). Let t 1 , … , t M + 1 denote the resulting segment boundary indices. From these, two derived sequences are constructed: segment durations (11) and net segment amplitudes

SampEn is then computed separately for the duration and amplitude sequences using the same Chebyshev-distance template matching criterion as in the SampEn analysis. To keep the similarity threshold relative to sequence variability, the tolerances are set as where SD(•) refers to standard deviation.

This yields entropy estimates following Equation (4).

In addition, a joint ExSEnt is computed by z-normalizing the duration and amplitude sequences (Equation 1), interleaving them into a single series where D z and A z denote the z-normalized duration and amplitude sequences, and estimating SampEn with embedding dimension 2m and tolerance r, following Equation (4).

Thus, ExSEnt preserves the standard SampEn definition but quantifies signal complexity in the temporal organization of extrema-defined durations and amplitudes, instead of in the raw signal or its coarse-grained representations.

2.1.4. Fractal dimension

Fractal dimension estimates the scale-free geometric complexity of a signal from a single scaling exponent, without pattern matching or coarse-graining. ASCENT includes two time-domain estimators, both computed for each channel [11]. The box-counting method quantifies how the number of boxes needed to cover the signal's graph scales with box size, whereas the Higuchi method estimates dimension from how the signal's mean curve length scales across subsampling intervals [37].

For the box-counting fractal dimension (FracDim) [11], the signal is first mapped to the unit square by normalizing both the time axis and amplitude to [0,1]. For each dyadic scale r j =2 -j , the time axis is partitioned into columns of width r j , and the number of vertical boxes required to cover the amplitude range within each occupied column is counted, which gives N ( r j ).

The fractal dimension is obtained from the log-log scaling relation, estimated in practice as the negative slope of a linear fit to { log r j , log N ( r j )} across valid dyadic scales.

The standard error of the slope is retained as an uncertainty measure. To improve robustness for EEG data, transient bursts are optionally identified and excluded using a sliding median absolute deviation (MAD) z-score on the amplitude, and scalewise slope outliers may be trimmed using an interquartile range criterion prior to the final regression. The slope is estimated using either ordinary least squares (OLS) or a robust Theil-Sen estimator [38].

Higuchi fractal dimension (HigFracDim) estimates fractal dimension from the scaling of mean curve length across multiple subsampling intervals [37]. For a time series x(1), …, x(N), and for each subsampling interval k = 1 , … , k max and starting offset m = 1, …, k, the normalized mean curve length is computed as and averaged over offsets as

The Higuchi fractal dimension is then the slope of the log-log scaling relation estimated by linear regression of log L(k) against log(1/k) across valid values of k, where c in Equation ( 20) is the intercept.

As with the box-counting method, the slope is estimated with a Theil-Sen robust estimator (default) or OLS, and the standard error (SE) of the slope is reported. The normalization uses ( ⌊ N-m)/k as in the original formulation by ⌋ Higuchi [37], instead of the rounded variant found in some implementations. The default is k max = 16. Since Higuchi estimates depend on k max , users should verify that the estimate is stable over the chosen range for their data [12]. Both methods share the same regression routine, which supports Theil-Sen robust fitting [38] with automatic fallback to OLS when fewer than the minimum number of valid scales are available.

2.2. Multiscale entropy measures

>Multiscale entropy measures

2.2.1. Multiscale entropy (MSE)

MSE extends single-scale entropy by computing SampEn on coarse-grained versions of the signal, each representing a progressively slower timescale. Hence, it provides a complexity profile instead of a single value [9]. MSE is computed independently for each EEG channel by evaluating SampEn across a family of coarse-grained sequences [9, 18, 35, 39]. Missing values are linearly interpolated per channel (nearest end-point filling), and the signal is z-normalized as in Equation (1). By default, the similarity bound r is defined relative to the SD of the original signal (default r = 0.15) and held constant across scales, as in the original formulations [9, 35]. Optionally, r can instead be recomputed at each scale from the SD of the coarse-grained sequence, as recommended by Kosciessa et al. [20], so that it remains a consistent fraction of the scale-specific variance instead of becoming increasingly permissive at coarser scales as signal variance decreases. For each scale factor s, the z-normalized signal is partitioned into N s =⌊ N / s ⌋ non-overlapping bins of length s, and a coarse-grained series is constructed by applying a coarse-graining operator C within each bin: where C denotes the bin mean (default), median, standard deviation, or variance.

MSE at each scale is then defined as: following Equation (4), where B m (r ) and A m + 1 (r ) denote the proportions of matching template pairs of length m and m+1 in y ( s) , respectively, excluding self-matches.

2.2.2. Multiscale fuzzy entropy (MFE)

MFE applies the same coarse-graining across scales but uses fuzzy entropy instead of SampEn, which improves robustness at coarse scales and in shorter recordings [18, 35]. MFE follows the same preprocessing and coarse-graining pipeline as MSE, with missing value interpolation, per-channel z-normalization, and the same similarity-bound conventions as described above. MFE at each scale is then computed as MFE ( s)=FuzzEn ( y ( s) ; m , r , n , τ )=ln ( φ m (r ) φ m + 1 (r ) ) (23) following Equation (9), where φ m (r ) and φ m + 1 (r ) denote the mean fuzzy similarity over all unique pairs of m-and (m+1)-dimensional embedded vectors of y ( s) , respectively.

2.2.3. Composite multiscale fuzzy entropy (CMFE)

CMFE extends MFE and reduces the variance of coarse-scale estimates by computing entropy from all shifted coarse-grained sequences at each scale and averaging the results [40]. Instead of computing FuzzEn from a single coarse-grained series at each scale s, CMFE forms all s shifted coarse-grained series by varying the starting offset α = 1, …, s:

FuzzEn is then computed separately for each shifted series following Equation ( 9), and the CMFE value at scale s is obtained by averaging those entropy estimates across offsets:

Thus, the only change relative to MFE is that entropy at each scale is estimated from the mean of the offset-specific FuzzEn values, instead of from a single coarse-grained sequence.

2.2.4. Refined composite MFE (RCMFE)

RCMFE further extends CMFE by changing the stage at which averaging across offsets is performed [35]. In CMFE, the final FuzzEn values are averaged across the s shifted coarse-grained series at each scale. In RCMFE, the underlying fuzzy similarity functions for embedding dimensions m and m+1 are first averaged across offsets, and entropy is then computed from those averaged quantities. Denoting the offset-specific similarity terms φ α m and φ α m + 1 as defined in Equations ( 8) and ( 24), RCMFE at scale s is defined as:

Accordingly, RCMFE differs from CMFE only in that averaging is applied to the similarity terms before taking the logarithmic ratio, and not to the final entropy values after that ratio is computed. This refined-composite formulation further improves stability, particularly at larger scales and for shorter time series [35].

2.2.5. Modified multiscale entropy (mMSE)

mMSE addresses two limitations of conventional multiscale entropy measures identified by Kosciessa et al. [20]. First, a similarity bound held fixed across scales becomes increasingly permissive as coarse-graining reduces signal variance. Second, at fine scales the full broadband signal contributes to entropy estimation, which in neural data means that low-frequency components dominate, so that fine-scale entropy does not isolate fast dynamics as conventionally assumed [20, 41]. Together, these issues can produce scalemismatched associations between entropy and spectral power that may be mistaken for genuine complexity effects. mMSE deals with these issues by normalizing the signal at each scale and by replacing statistical coarse-graining with a spectral coarse-graining procedure ("filt-skip") in which the signal is filtered to each scale-specific frequency band before decimation. For each scale factor s ≥ 2, the z-normalized signal z(t) is bandpass filtered within the band: where f Nyq =f s /2 is the Nyquist frequency (in practice, each band edge is widened by 5% to limit attenuation at the edges).

After filtering, the signal is rescaled to unit variance (so that the similarity bound r is effectively recomputed at each scale) and decimated by a factor of s using s staggered phase offsets. This gives s downsampled sequences y k ( s) , k = 1 , … , s. SampEn is computed for each sequence and averaged across offsets:

This averaging across phase offsets follows the composite logic of CMFE (Equation ( 25)) and reduces estimation variance at coarser scales compared with single-phase pointskipping. By construction, entropy at each scale reflects the irregularity of signal components within a defined frequency band. This allows a more direct comparison with spectral measures, and scale-specific effects are easier to interpret. ASCENT implements the bandpass "filt-skip" scheme as the default, but the standard statistical coarse-graining mode is also available for direct comparability with standard MSE.

This bandpass scheme is modeled on Kosciessa et al.'s bandpass filter option, as opposed to their lowpass default, which filters to [ 0 , f Nyq / s ] at each scale. The lowpass approach prevents aliasing but retains all sub-cutoff slow dynamics, so fine-scale entropy still reflects low-frequency dominance. The bandpass variant removes this content more completely. ASCENT differs from Kosciessa et al. in three respects. The passband spans the whole interval between successive scale cutoffs (Equation (27)) instead of ±5% around the lowpass cutoff, entropy is averaged over starting points instead of being computed from pooled match counts, and filtering uses zero-phase finite impulse response (FIR) filters instead of Chebyshev and Butterworth infinite impulse response (IIR) filters.

A time-resolved mode is also available, inspired by the sliding-window approach of Kloosterman and colleagues [41] and applied here to consecutive windows of one continuous recording. Entropy is estimated within windows of configurable duration (e.g., 10 s with 50% overlap; disabled by default) stepped across the recording, which gives a continuous measure of signal complexity as a function of both time and scale. To ensure stable estimation, the maximum number of scales is automatically capped so that each scale retains a minimum number of samples after decimation, and scales falling below this threshold are excluded.

2.2.6. Shared conventions

All entropy measures in ASCENT share the following conventions: (1) signals are znormalized per channel prior to analysis (Equation 1); (2) delay-embedded vectors are constructed as in Equation ( 2) with configurable embedding dimension m and lag τ; (3) inter-vector distances use the Chebyshev norm (Equation 3); (4) by default, the similarity bound r is defined relative to the SD of the original signal (default r = 0.15); ( 5) missing (non-finite) samples are handled by linear interpolation or exclusion; (6) all implementations can optionally run in parallel.

For univariate multiscale measures, r can optionally be recomputed at each scale from the coarse-grained sequence, so that it remains a consistent fraction of scale-specific variance. This scale-wise normalization is applied by default only in mMSE. The maximum number of scales S is automatically capped so that every scale retains a minimum number of samples, and individual scales failing this criterion are excluded. Scale s = 1 is excluded by default from the univariate multiscale outputs, as it is mathematically equivalent to the corresponding single-scale measure (SampEn or FuzzEn). For the SD and variance operators, it is also degenerate, since the SD of a singlesample bin is identically zero.

Four operators are available for constructing coarse-grained sequences: the bin mean, median, standard deviation (SD), and variance. Mean-based coarse-graining (the default), introduced by Costa et al. [9], characterizes the irregularity of scale-dependent average dynamics, whereas SD-based coarse-graining, introduced by Azami et al. [35], quantifies the complexity of within-bin fluctuation structure, which reflects intermittency and volatility at each scale. Note that these operators are complementary and not interchangeable.

2.3. Multivariate entropy measures

>Multivariate entropy measures mvFuzzEn extends univariate FuzzEn to the multivariate case by treating all channels as a single high-dimensional system, in which delayed samples from all channels are embedded jointly.

2.3.1. Multivariate fuzzy entropy (mvFuzzEn)

It thus quantifies the collective complexity of their shared dynamics, as opposed to pairwise interactions [42, 43]. Signals are z-normalized per channel as in Equation (1). Given per-channel embedding dimensions M = [m 1 , ..., m K ] and time lags τ = [τ 1 , ..., τ K ], joint delay vectors are constructed by concatenating delayed samples from all K channels: the same vectors are available at dimension m+1), and each vector has dimension ∑ k m k.

Each embedded vector is mean-centered across all of its elements (as in Equation ( 5)), distances are computed using the Chebyshev norm as in Equation (3), and fuzzy similarities are computed using the exponential kernel of Equation ( 6). This gives φ m (r ) as defined in Equation ( 8) applied to the joint multivariate vectors.

To extend to dimension m+1, K augmented embedding matrices are formed by incrementing the embedding dimension of one channel h at a time while holding all others fixed. The fuzzy similarity φ h m + 1 (r ) is computed separately for each augmented subspace h = 1, …, K, and φ m + 1 (r ) is defined as the mean across subspaces, mvFuzzEn is then defined as in Equation ( 9), substituting the multivariate φ m and φ m + 1.

Values are set to NaN when either similarity term is zero or non-finite, and negative values are valid when φ m + 1 (r ) > φ m (r ) [42,43].

The present implementation replaces the original naive full-matrix pairwise distance computation with bounded-memory block-wise accumulation of pairwise kernel sums, so that the full distance matrix is never instantiated. For the comparison pooled across the K subspaces that the reference code performs (retained in RCmvMFE, Section 2.3.2) and a typical EEG recording (e.g., K = 5 channels, N = 19,200 samples, i.e., 75 s at 256 Hz), a naive KN × KN pairwise distance matrix requires approximately 68.7 GiB (73.7 GB) of memory in double precision, which caused the reference implementation to crash before returning a result. The present implementation remains tractable under the same conditions without requiring high-memory computing infrastructure.

2.3.2. Refined composite multivariate MFE (RCmvMFE)

RCmvMFE extends mvFuzzEn to multiple temporal scales using the same joint delay embedding, Chebyshev distance, and exponential kernel described above [42, 43]. Note that its implementation differs from the uniscale mvFuzzEn in two ways. First, the similarity bound follows the original multivariate convention and is set as r = r 0 ∑ k SD k , where SD k is the standard deviation of channel k and r0 = 0.15, so that r = r 0 K after z- normalization. The threshold is thus adapted to the dimensionality of the joint embedding space instead of being held fixed. Second, φ m + 1 is computed by pooling all K augmented embedding matrices into a single KN-row matrix before computing pairwise similarities, instead of averaging K separate per-subspace estimates as in mvFuzzEn.

For each scale factor s, s multivariate coarse-grained series are generated using starting offsets α = 1, …, s, following the same offset coarse-graining logic as RCMFE (Equation ( 24)). Fuzzy similarities φ α m and φ α m + 1 are computed for each offset, accumulated across all s offsets, and RCmvMFE at scale s is defined as

This pooling follows the same logic as RCMFE (Equation 26). Unlike the univariate multiscale measures, scale s = 1 is retained for mean and median coarse-graining (it is excluded for SD and variance). Unlike mvFuzzEn, embedded vectors are not meancentered before distance computation. All four coarse-graining operators are supported. The memory and performance improvements described for mvFuzzEn above apply here as well.

2.4. Aperiodic (1/f) exponent and offset

Aperiodic activity is characterized by fitting the power spectrum with a broadband 1/f component (exponent and offset) plus Gaussian peaks, following the spectral parameterization (specparam) approach, so that oscillatory peaks are isolated without relying on predefined frequency bands [13]. Power spectral density (PSD) estimation is performed per channel using Welch's method, with a Hann-windowed segment length of w seconds (default 4 s, i.e., a frequency resolution of 0.25 Hz), 50% overlap, and a fast Fourier transform (FFT) length rounded up to the next power of two. Linear detrending is applied to the full signal prior to spectral estimation. The resulting one-sided linear PSD (in µV²/Hz) is passed without log transformation to the aperiodic fitting routine, following the specparam convention. Welch's method was chosen over a single-segment FFT because its smoother spectra may contain fewer noise fluctuations that can be misidentified as periodic peaks, as suggested for task-based data [44]. Aperiodic fitting proceeds iteratively in log-power space over a specified frequency range. The aperiodic component is modeled as where b is the broadband offset, χ (chi) is the exponent, and κ (kappa) is an optional knee parameter controlling bends in the aperiodic component at broad frequency ranges.

The fitting algorithm follows seven steps: (1) an initial robust aperiodic fit following specparam, in which a first fit is refined by refitting only the frequencies whose power lies at or below it, so that spectral peaks do not bias the fit (least squares in fixed mode; nonlinear least squares in knee mode); ( 2 The maximum number of extractable peaks was set to P max = 3, because the internal consistency of aperiodic estimates decreases, and the number of physiologically implausible positive slope values increases, as more peaks are allowed [44]. Note that three peaks was the largest setting tested in that study and that reliability was highest when no peak was fitted, so users who favor reliability may lower this value. The value P max = 3 also matches the settings used in the SPRiNT reference implementation [45].

Default parameters otherwise follow [13] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ngCbIA frequency range 1-40 Hz, minimum peak height h min = 0.05, and peak threshold σ min = 2.0. Peak width limits default to [1, 12] Hz, which is wider than Donoghue et al.'s EEG recommendation of [1, 6] Hz to accommodate broader peaks that may arise in resting-state recordings. Optionally, the fitted aperiodic model is subtracted from the log-transformed PSD to yield an aperiodic-corrected spectrum isolating periodic components: which is then converted back to linear scale.

The correction is implemented for both fitting modes. In knee mode, the fitted Lorentzian model (offset, knee, exponent) is subtracted in full, as in the internal "flattened spectrum" computation of the reference specparam implementation. The correction removes broadband 1/f structure so that spectral analyses on the corrected PSD emphasize periodic activity. Because it divides the PSD by the aperiodic fit (a subtraction in log power, as in specparam), it assumes that periodic power scales multiplicatively with the aperiodic background, whereas a linear subtraction would yield absolute periodic power. The two can differ when the background changes between conditions.

Because aperiodic activity is not stationary across time [17] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?A388dQ time-varying estimation is implemented following the SPRiNT architecture [45] via ASCENT's compute_AperiodicFit_sliding function. Short Hann-windowed FFT segments of length w slid seconds (default 2 s, i.e., 0.5 Hz frequency resolution) are computed across the full signal with a fractional overlap of δ slid (default 50%), which gives a step of 1 s between consecutive segments. At each time bin, the power spectra of n avg consecutive segments (default 5) are averaged to produce a spectrally smoothed PSD estimate. This separates frequency resolution (controlled by w slid ) from the spectral signal-to-noise ratio (controlled by n avg ). The aperiodic model is then fitted to each smoothed PSD to obtain continuous exponent(t) and offset(t) traces for each channel. Peak width limits for the sliding fit are set to [2, 8] Hz, well above the recommended minimum of twice the frequency resolution (1 Hz for 2-s windows) and matching the settings of Gyurkovics et al. [17]. Following SPRiNT's recommended post-processing, periodic peaks that do not recur across neighboring time bins (fewer than 3 similar peaks within 2.5 Hz and ±6 time bins) are removed, and the aperiodic model is refit at the affected time bins [45].

2.5. Visualizations

ASCENT provides integrated visualization for all entropy, complexity, and aperiodic measures via the ascent_plot function, which automatically selects the appropriate display based on data dimensionality. For single-scale multichannel measures, a scalp topography is displayed. For single-channel multiscale measures, an entropy-by-scale curve is shown. For scalar measures such as mvFuzzEn, a bar display is used with an explicit note when negative entropy values are returned.

For multichannel multiscale data, results are displayed as a channel-by-scale entropy heatmap alongside up to three automatically detected high-entropy clusters (see Fig. 2). Cluster detection is scale-first and channel-order-agnostic to avoid bias from arbitrary channel ordering. First, the per-scale mean entropy across all channels is computed. Scales whose mean reaches a user-defined percentile of the per-scale means (default: 75th percentile) are grouped into contiguous segments. Within each segment, channels are retained if their mean entropy over that scale range reaches the same percentile of all finite channel-by-scale values. The resulting clusters are sorted by total entropy mass, and the top three are kept. If no cluster satisfies the criteria, the single channel-scale pair with the highest entropy is displayed instead. Cluster boundaries are overlaid on the heatmap as smoothed contour lines in distinct colors, one per cluster. Since the members of a cluster need not be adjacent in the channel (or IC) list, one cluster can be outlined by several boxes. For each cluster, a scalp topography of the mean entropy over the cluster's scale range is shown, together with the mean entropy curve across all scales for the cluster's channels. When clusters differ meaningfully in their scale coverage, the curve's scale extent is shaded with the cluster color to mark the range over which the cluster was defined.

For multiscale multichannel entropy data computed in independent component (IC) space (see Fig. 3), we first identify clusters of ICs that share a common scale-resolved entropy profile. Clusters are detected by thresholding the per-scale mean entropy across ICs at a user-defined percentile (default 75th) and then finding contiguous scale ranges. Within each range, ICs whose mean entropy exceeds the same percentile are retained. This scale-first, IC-order-agnostic procedure avoids bias from arbitrary IC ordering. For each cluster, three visualizations are generated: (i) a bar chart of per-IC mean entropy over the cluster's scale extent, (ii) the mean entropy curve across scales for all ICs in the cluster, and (iii) a back-projected scalp topography. Back-projection follows the EEGLAB convention, e scalp =W -1 e IC , where W -1 is the ICA mixing matrix and e IC is the vector of per-IC mean entropy over the cluster's scale range. Note that this linear mapping is not a source localization, and because the polarity of each IC is arbitrary, the map depends on the polarity convention of the decomposition and should only be read qualitatively. It simply shows how the entropy "weights" would be distributed on the sensors (i.e., a familiar scalp-space view of the cluster's spatial signature). When DIPFIT equivalent-dipole fits are available, a companion figure is automatically generated for every measure computed on ICs except the multivariate ones (see Fig. 3 for RCMFE). The dipole fitting uses a realistic head model to solve the EEG forward problem, explicitly accounting for volume conduction, and searches for the equivalent current dipole whose forward-projected scalp potential best matches the IC's scalp topography. Following the EEGLAB convention, only ICs with residual variance < 15% are considered, so that the single-dipole approximation is valid and the source is likely focal. The fitted dipoles of all dipolar ICs located inside the brain are rendered on a standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) MRI (dipoles outside the brain compartment of the head model come from artifactual ICs, such as eye or muscle components, and are not shown). Each dipole is colored by the value of the measure for its IC (the mean across scales for multiscale measures), and its size increases with the goodness of fit (1 -residual variance). When ICLabel classifications are available, ICs classified as brain are drawn as circles and the others as squares, and the number of brain ICs in the cluster is reported. Each dipole is also labeled with the region of the automated anatomical labeling (AAL) atlas that contains it, or the nearest region within 10 mm [46], and these regions are grouped into lobes. These labels, the residual variances, and the ICLabel classes of all ICs are printed in the command window and saved with the results, and the values are plotted by lobe (with mean curves across scales for multiscale measures) for lobes containing at least three ICs. Last, ASCENT checks the coregistration of the channel locations with the head model and warns users when the montage is rotated by 90° relative to the MNI template, as happens when EEGLAB channel coordinates (nose along the x-axis) are used without a coordinate transformation. Since ICs are not selected by their entropy for this display, it introduces no circularity.

For the aperiodic measure, two display modes are available: -In the static mode (see Fig. 4, left panel), scalp topographies of the aperiodic exponent and offset are shown (back-projected to sensor space if ICA is enabled). A scatter plot of exponent versus offset across channels (or ICs) is provided, with a linear regression line and correlation coefficient, to show how these two aperiodic parameters naturally covary (steeper spectra tend to have higher offsets) and to flag any channels or components that fall far from the main trend, which may indicate poor fits or artifacts. When ICA is used, the IC with the largest exponent is highlighted. The mean raw and corrected PSDs are plotted (log₁₀ power against frequency) as mean ± SD across channels/ICs, together with the fitted 1/f slopes (dashed lines). Scalp topographies of alpha-band power (8-13 Hz) are displayed by default, both before and after subtracting the aperiodic fit. In ICA mode, these panels show the alpha power of the IC with the maximum exponent, projected to the scalp through its mixing weights. -In the time-resolved mode (SPRiNT-style; see Figs. 4 and 5, right panels), timefrequency spectrograms of the raw and, if available, corrected PSD are shown as heatmaps of the mean log-power across channels/ICs. The time courses of the aperiodic exponent and offset are plotted as mean ± SD across channels/ICs on dual y-axes. Finally, band-averaged power trajectories for theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), and beta (13-30 Hz) are overlaid. When a corrected PSD is supplied, raw (dashed) and corrected (solid) band averages are drawn on separate y-axes (raw power on the left, power relative to the aperiodic fit on the right), since the two are different quantities.

Current visualization support is limited to channel-level and IC back-projected data. Intracranial or source-localized visualizations are under development for future releases.

2.6. Diagnostics

To validate numerical equivalence between ASCENT's optimized implementations and the original reference algorithms, output values were compared channel-by-channel for SampEn, FuzzEn, ExSEnt, and MSE on the same 64-channel EEG dataset (the remaining measures could not be compared without extensive additional programming work or, for the multivariate measures, because the reference implementations exceeded available memory).

Note that more details on algorithmic correctness and validation can be found in the original studies from which each measure is directly adapted [9, 13, 18, 20, [33] [34] [35] [36] [37] [40] [41] [42] [43] [44]. The goal of this manuscript and toolbox is not to re-validate them but to make them easily available and interpretable to the community.

To validate the aperiodic parameterization specifically, ASCENT's MATLAB implementation of the specparam algorithm was benchmarked against the official Python specparam reference (v2.0.0rc6) on matched settings (fixed mode, 1-40 Hz, peak width limits [1, 12] Hz, maximum 3 peaks), using both synthetic spectra with known ground truth (n = 200) and the 64 real Welch spectra of the sample dataset (Supplementary Figure S1). The two implementations agreed closely on real EEG (exponent and offset: r > 0.999, mean absolute difference ≤ 0.001, 95% limits of agreement within ±0.01) and on synthetic spectra (r > 0.999 for both parameters, with an identical number of fitted peaks for all 200 spectra), and they recovered the ground-truth parameters equally well (exponent: r = 0.938; offset: r = 0.970 for both). The few remaining differences (≤ 0.03) arose from optimizer differences in multi-peak joint fits.

2.7. Subject-level illustration

The plugin contains a 75-s, 64-channel BioSemi EEG dataset (256 Hz) taken from [47], subject ID "3011e6c715". It was preprocessed with the same pipeline as the group-level data (Section 2.8).

We provide the ascent_group_analysis script, which documents the preprocessing of the group dataset and runs the group analysis. We also provide a detailed tutorial, called ascent_tutorial, to guide users through the installation of the plugin, dataset loading, and various ways to use the plugin and compute the measures available via both the GUI and command line, on both scalp EEG data and independent component (IC) time series. Here we show briefly how to compute one multiscale measure (with two coarse-graining methods), in scalp channel space and in IC space, as well as the aperiodic-corrected PSD (Fig. 1C) on the sample dataset for illustration and replication.

In the first GUI pop-up window (Fig. 1A), we keep all the default parameters to compute the refined composite multiscale fuzzy entropy (RCMFE) on all EEG channels, with visualization, progress tracking and parallel computing all turned on.

In the second GUI (Fig. 1B), which pops up automatically, we keep the default parameters ("Mean" coarse-graining, τ = 1 (time lag), m = 2 (embedding dimension), and n = 2 (fuzzy power)) and set the number of scale factors to 50 (default: 30). Fig. 1B shows this window with its default settings ("Mean" coarse-graining and 30 scale factors).

When completed, we repeat the same steps, and change the coarse-graining to "Std" (Standard deviation) instead of "Mean" (50 scales as well), for comparison.

Next, to illustrate the ICA mode, ICA was performed on the same sample dataset prior to entropy estimation. RCMFE was then computed directly on the IC time series over 30 scale factors with standard deviation coarse-graining. IC-domain computation is available both from the GUI (by selecting "ICA components" as the data domain in the first window) and from the command line (see the ascent_tutorial script provided with the toolbox).

Fig. 1. A) Main graphical user interface (GUI) pop-up window, where users load a dataset (or the sample dataset provided with the plugin) if none is loaded in EEGLAB, choose the measure to compute, the data to use (scalp channels or ICA components) and the EEG channels of interest, and turn on visualizations, progress tracking, and parallel computing. B) Second GUI, which pops up when users choose to compute a complexity/entropy measure, to select τ (the time lag) and m (the embedding dimension). If a multiscale measure was selected, they can select the coarse-graining method (mean, median, standard deviation, or variance), the number of scale factors, and n, the fuzzy power value (for fuzzy entropy measures only). C) Third GUI, shown when aperiodic mode is selected in the first GUI, for setting PSD estimation parameters (frequency range, window length), aperiodic fitting options (mode, peak count and width limits), whether to subtract the aperiodic component from the PSD, and whether to compute the time-resolved (SPRiNT-style) aperiodic fit. Note: parameters that do not apply to some measures are grayed out automatically, based on the users' choices.

2.8. Group-level illustration

We tested ASCENT v2.1 (2026) on a group dataset of research-grade, 64-channel resting-state EEG comparing eyes-closed (EC) and eyes-open (EO) recordings of approximately 1 minute each (mean 68 s per condition; N = 40; see [47] for collection details). Preprocessing was performed in EEGLAB v2025 under MATLAB R2025b, and included downsampling to 256 Hz, BEM 10-05 electrode coordinate assignment, REST rereferencing [48], high-pass FIR filtering at 1 Hz (zero-phase noncausal; order = 846; transition bandwidth = 1 Hz; -6 dB at 0.5 Hz), low-pass FIR filtering at 50 Hz (zero-phase noncausal; order = 68; transition bandwidth = 12.5 Hz; -6 dB at 56.25 Hz), which also attenuated the 60 Hz power-line noise, artifact correction via ASR (burst criterion = 40; bursts were reconstructed and no segment was removed), spherical interpolation of rejected channels, and ICA decomposition using Picard [30] with rank-matched decomposition [49]. Artifactual components were labeled and removed using ICLabel [50] (muscle ≥ 0.90, eye ≥ 0.90, cardiac ≥ 0.95, line noise ≥ 0.95, channel noise ≥ 0.90).

Most ASCENT measures were computed per subject: SampEn, FuzzEn, ExSEnt (HD, HA, HDA), Higuchi fractal dimension (HigFracDim), aperiodic exponent and offset, MSE, mMSE, MFE, and RCMFE. The two multivariate measures were excluded to reduce computational cost, and because they are not directly comparable with the other measures as they provide a single output for all EEG channels. The box-counting fractal dimension and CMFE were not included either. Multiscale measures were computed with 30 scale factors using both mean and standard deviation coarse-graining (scales 2-30; RCMFE with mean coarse-graining also included scale 1). At the time of the group analysis, MSE and MFE normalized each coarse-grained sequence before entropy estimation (i.e., scalewise tolerance), RCMFE used a fixed similarity bound, and mMSE used its default bandpass filtering with scale-wise normalization (in this mode mMSE does not use a coarse-graining operator, so it was computed and tested once). PSDs and aperiodic parameters were computed with the current default settings (Section 2.4).

All statistical analyses were performed outside the ASCENT interface on the exported outputs, using the open-source code described in Section 1.3 [32]. Group differences between conditions were assessed using mass-univariate nonparametric paired t-tests with 2,000 permutations [51, 52] at α = 0.05, corrected for family-wise error (FWE) using cluster-based correction [51, 53]. Clusters were formed from adjacent channels (single-scale measures) or adjacent channel-by-scale cells (multiscale measures) with uncorrected two-sided p < 0.05 irrespective of sign (cells with fewer than two significant neighboring channels were discarded), cluster mass was defined as the sum of absolute t-values, and each observed cluster was compared with the permutation distribution of the maximum cluster mass. Differences in raw and aperiodic-corrected power spectral density (PSD, in dB; channels × frequencies) were assessed using the same methods.

Channel adjacency was defined using Delaunay triangulation of the (2-D projected) electrode positions. For single-scale measures, we report the significant channels and the peak channel. For multiscale measures and PSDs, a custom routine splits each significant region by the sign of t, groups same-sign cells that overlap in scale or frequency, and reports the bounds, peak channel and statistic of each part. Because cluster mass is computed on absolute t-values, one significant region can contain effects of opposite sign, and these sign-specific parts, their extents and their peaks are descriptive. Cluster-based inference supports a difference within a cluster but not its exact borders, and effect sizes at cluster peaks are biased upward by the selection of the maximum. Effect sizes are given as Hedges' g for paired comparisons (standardized by the SD of the paired differences), computed as g = t √n ( 1 -3 4 (n -1) -1 ) , where n is the number of participants.

To characterize inter-measure redundancy and spatial divergence between the single-scale measures, two descriptive correlation analyses were conducted. In the first, an EC -EO difference score was computed per channel and per subject for each measure. Each difference matrix was then averaged across channels to yield one scalar per subject per measure, and global pairwise Spearman correlations were computed across subjects for all measure pairs. This matrix captures the extent to which subjects showing a larger condition-related shift in one measure also show a larger shift in another (i.e., individuallevel covariance in EC -EO reactivity, averaged across the scalp).

In the second analysis, pairwise Spearman correlations were computed across channels between the t-value maps derived from the single-scale paired permutation tests for each measure pair. This spatial correlation matrix captures the degree to which each pair of measures localizes condition effects to the same scalp regions at the group level. These spatial correlations are descriptive, since neighboring channels are not independent and the effective number of observations is well below 64.

3. Results

>Results

3.1. Diagnostics

To verify that the optimized implementations give the same values as the original algorithms, the ASCENT implementations were benchmarked against their original reference algorithms on the same 64-channel dataset. Output values were compared channel-by-channel for SampEn, FuzzEn, ExSEnt, and MSE. For Sample Entropy and Fuzzy Entropy, differences were uniformly on the order of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁵, as expected from a difference in normalization (ASCENT computes match proportions over all templates of each length, whereas the reference implementations use the same number of templates for both lengths, which changes the estimate by a term of order 1/N). For ExSEnt (joint estimate), differences were consistent in sign and on the order of 10⁻⁴ (+2 to +3 × 10⁻⁴), a systematic offset that comes from the same normalization (ASCENT takes the ratio of match proportions and the reference the ratio of raw match counts). For MSE, the two benchmark runs differed in their tolerance setting. At 5 scales, the benchmarked version of ASCENT normalized each coarse-grained sequence before entropy estimation (scalewise tolerance, as recommended by Kosciessa et al. [20]), whereas the reference implementation [9] holds the tolerance fixed across scales, and absolute differences reached ~0.36. At 50 scales, run with a fixed tolerance as in the reference, differences were below 0.002 at scales 2 to 6 and mostly below 10⁻² (maximum ~0.09 at the coarsest scales, where few samples remain). Overall, these results indicate that ASCENT's optimized SampEn, FuzzEn, and ExSEnt implementations are numerically equivalent to their reference counterparts (i.e., the performance gains come from restructuring the computations instead of approximating the algorithms), and that the MSE differences at 5 scales are due to the choice of tolerance.

Computation time was reduced for all benchmarked measures: Sample Entropy from 10.28 s to 3.49 s (~3× speedup), Fuzzy Entropy from 13.92 s to 11.54 s (~1.2× speedup), and Multiscale Entropy (MSE) from 84.44 s to 5.40 s at 5 scales (~16×) and from 104.55 s to 6.01 s at 50 scales (~17×). Note that the computational demand of the original implementation grows with the number of scales. The largest gain was observed for Extrema-Segmented Entropy (ExSEnt), which dropped from 397.25 s to 6.15 s (~65× speedup).

For the multivariate measures (mvFuzzEn and RCmvMFE), the reference implementations could not be completed on typical hardware even for a 5-channel subset of the sample recording (N = 19,200 samples), as the naive full-matrix pairwise distance computation required approximately 69 GiB of RAM and exhausted available memory before returning a result. ASCENT's block-wise accumulation implementation completed the corresponding computation in under 60 s on a standard desktop workstation, so that multivariate fuzzy entropy can be computed on EEG recordings of realistic length without high-memory computers. These improvements were achieved through algorithmic vectorization, elimination of redundant per-channel loops, and optional parallelization via MATLAB's Parallel Computing Toolbox (MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA, USA).

3.2. Subject level

>Subject level

3.2.1. Multiscale entropy illustrations

RCMFE was computed across 50 scale factors (scales 2-50) and 64 EEG channels on the 75-s resting-state dataset provided with the ASCENT plugin (one subject; see Fig. 2). Two coarse-graining operators were compared. Using mean coarse-graining (Fig. 2, top), a single widespread cluster was detected at fine-to-intermediate scales (63 channels × 12 scales, scales 4-15), with peak entropy at channel P8 at scale 9. Using standard deviation coarse-graining (Fig. 2, bottom), a single cluster was detected at coarser scales (33 channels × 12 scales, scales 19-30) with a centroparietal distribution, peaking at channel CP4 at scale 29. Note that these clusters are percentile-based and descriptive (Section 2.5), with no statistical test. Hence, the two coarse-graining operators resulted in clusters with different spatial and scale distributions for the same subject and recording. Top: Mean coarse-graining. Bottom: Standard deviation coarse-graining. The scalp topographies show the mean entropy over each cluster's scale range, and the curves show the cluster-mean entropy across scale factors. Clusters (orange outlines) are defined with the default 75th-percentile rule (Section 2.5); a cluster is outlined by several boxes when its channels are not adjacent in the channel list. See Section 3.2.1 for details.

Fig. 3 shows the IC-domain RCMFE output for the same sample dataset. A single cluster was detected, comprising 30 ICs across 7 scale factors (scales 5-11), with its centroid (the IC with the highest mean entropy over these scales) at IC40 and its peak at scale 6. The cluster entropy curve peaked at early-to-intermediate timescales (scales ~5-6) and declined monotonically at coarser scales. The back-projected scalp topography showed a posterior-dominant distribution (which depends on the IC polarity convention; Section 2.5). Only 3 of the 30 cluster ICs had acceptable dipole fits (residual variance < 15%; most had between 30 and 94%), so Fig. 3 (bottom) shows the equivalent dipoles of all dipolar ICs of the decomposition located inside the brain (n = 18) on the MNI template. In the AAL atlas, eight of them were in or near the cingulate cortex, three in the parietal lobe, and the others in temporal, occipital, or deep regions (two at the level of the brainstem, outside the AAL regions). Single dipoles fit on a template head model tend to be placed too deep, so these labels are approximate (Section 4.4). ICLabel classified 17 of these 18 ICs as brain. In contrast, it classified only 9 of the 30 cluster ICs as brain (median brain probability 0.17), against 23 of the other 29 ICs (median 0.93). Most cluster ICs fell in the "Other" class (n = 16), which ICLabel uses for components it cannot attribute to one source type, and they had a small back-projected variance (median 0.7% of the total per IC, against 1.9% for the other ICs). In this dataset, the highest RCMFE values thus came mostly from low-variance components that were neither dipolar nor clearly brain. with the detected cluster outlined in orange (several boxes, since its ICs are not adjacent in the list). (Top right) Mean entropy per IC averaged over the cluster scale extent, with cluster-member ICs highlighted in orange and the centroid IC (IC40) marked in red. Black dots mark the ICs that ICLabel classified as brain. Below it, mean entropy as a function of scale averaged across all cluster ICs (left) and the cluster-mean entropy back-projected onto the scalp via the ICA mixing matrix (scales 5-11, right). (Bottom) Equivalent dipoles of all ICs with a residual variance (RV) below 15% and a dipole inside the brain (n = 18) on the MNI template, in coronal, axial, and sagittal views. Marker color shows the mean entropy of each IC across scales, marker size the goodness of fit (1 -RV), and marker shape the ICLabel class (circles: brain; squares: other classes).

3.2.2. Aperiodic spectral parameterization illustrations

Fig. 4 (left panel) shows the aperiodic parameterization of the same dataset in the channel domain. Both the exponent and offset were highest over posterior and midline sites and lowest over lateral temporal sites. The two parameters are strongly correlated across channels (r = 0.90), as expected. The PSD plot shows the characteristic 1/f power decrease with frequency in the raw spectrum, which is largely flattened after aperiodic correction, while a prominent alpha peak remains visible in both. Alpha-band power (8-13 Hz) shows a posterior maximum in the raw PSD. After correction, frontal channels show little alpha-band power above the aperiodic fit, so the posterior predominance of alpha becomes more pronounced. On average across channels, about 17% of the alphaband power (12.3 µV²/Hz) was attributable to the aperiodic component (i.e., 10.2 µV²/Hz was above the aperiodic fit).

Fig. 4 (right panel) shows the time-resolved aperiodic parameterization across the 75-s recording. The raw PSD spectrogram shows a stable spectral structure over time, dominated by a prominent alpha-band ridge around 8-9 Hz. This ridge persists in the corrected spectrogram, where the broadband aperiodic slope is removed. The corrected values represent power relative to the aperiodic fit (dimensionless ratio), so their fluctuation around zero is due to the removal of the broadband background, while transient deflections reflect oscillatory dynamics. Both the exponent and offset show gradual fluctuations over time (exponent 1.11 ± 0.41; offset 1.30 ± 0.36, mean ± SD across channels and time bins, close to the static estimates of 1.16 ± 0.38 and 1.44 ± 0.24) while remaining relatively stable overall. The band-averaged power trajectories show raw (dashed, left axis) and corrected (solid, right axis) power in each band. Because the corrected traces are expressed relative to the aperiodic fit (right axis), their absolute level is not comparable to the raw traces, and their fluctuations may better isolate genuine oscillatory dynamics. Time courses of the aperiodic exponent (left axis) and offset (right axis), shown as the cross-channel mean ± SD at each time window. (Bottom) Time courses of mean ± SD band power for theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), and beta (13-30 Hz). Dashed lines: raw band power (left axis, log₁₀ µV²/Hz). Solid lines: aperiodic-corrected band power (right axis, log₁₀ power relative to the aperiodic fit; a dimensionless ratio). The two axes are separate quantities and not on a shared scale.

Fig. 5 shows the equivalent ICA-domain aperiodic analysis. In the top left panel, the per-IC exponents and offsets are back-projected onto the scalp through the ICA mixing matrix (arbitrary units). The exponent shows a right posterior maximum and the offset a right lateral (frontotemporal) maximum. The exponent-offset correlation across ICs remains strong (r = 0.85; left panel, middle top), and IC53 is highlighted as the component with the highest aperiodic exponent. As in the channel domain, the PSD plot (left panel, middle bottom) shows the characteristic 1/f power decrease with frequency in the raw spectrum, which is largely flattened after aperiodic correction, while a prominent alpha peak remains visible in both. The bottom maps show IC53's alpha-band power (8-13 Hz) projected to the scalp. Because a single IC has a fixed scalp projection, the raw and corrected maps share the same topography (a broad frontal maximum with bilateral temporal minima) and differ only in scale. For IC53, 78% of the alpha-band power was attributable to the aperiodic component, and on average across ICs, about half (46%).

The right panel shows a time-resolved structure similar to Fig. 4, with the alphaband ridge and stable aperiodic dynamics preserved across the recording (exponent 0.69 ± 0.35; offset -0.77 ± 0.57, mean ± SD across ICs and time bins). Aperiodic correction similarly removes broadband power differences between bands. Offsets are not comparable with the channel domain because IC activations are expressed in arbitrary units set by the ICA scaling. Exponents, which are unaffected by amplitude scaling, were lower on average than in the channel domain, which indicates flatter spectra for many individual components than for channel mixtures.

3.3. Group level

>Group level

3.3.1. Single-scale measures

Paired permutation tests (2,000 iterations, cluster-based correction over channel space) showed significant spatial clusters for all eight measures (see Fig. 6). Three measures showed negative clusters (EC < EO) spanning the full 64-channel array: SampEn (peak: F2, t = -9.51, Hedges' g = -1.47), FuzzEn (peak: FC3, t = -8.42, Hedges' g = -1.31), and HigFracDim (peak: F3, t = -10.32, Hedges' g = -1.60). ExSEnt Amplitude also yielded a negative cluster, over 43 frontocentral and posterior channels (peak: AFz, t = -5.72, Hedges' g = -0.89).

In contrast, four measures showed positive clusters (EC > EO). ExSEnt Duration produced a cluster over all 64 channels (peak: AFz, t = 9.90, Hedges' g = 1.54), and the aperiodic offset a near-global cluster of 61 channels that spared O1, Oz, and Iz (peak: F3, t = 6.53, Hedges' g = 1.01). The aperiodic exponent yielded a cluster of 53 channels that spared midline parietal and occipital sites (peak: AF3, t = 5.64, Hedges' g = 0.87), and ExSEnt Duration + Amplitude a cluster of 63 channels (all but P2; peak: Fp1, t = 8.83, Hedges' g = 1.37). To quantify inter-measure redundancy and divergence, two Spearman correlation analyses were performed on the single-scale results (Fig. 7). The global correlation matrix of channel-averaged EC -EO difference scores (Fig. 7A) showed strong positive coupling between SampEn and FuzzEn (rho = 0.89) and between the aperiodic exponent and offset (rho = 0.86). SampEn and FuzzEn each correlated positively with HigFracDim (rho = 0.60 and 0.52, respectively) and negatively with ExSEnt(HD) (rho = -0.84 and -0.66) and with both aperiodic parameters (SampEn: rho = -0.56 and -0.52; FuzzEn: rho = -0.68 and -0.64). ExSEnt(HD) showed moderate positive coupling with ExSEnt(HDA) (rho = 0.68) and negative coupling with HigFracDim (rho = -0.62). ExSEnt(HA) showed the weakest intermeasure coupling overall (|rho| ≤ 0.48), including weak associations with both aperiodic parameters (rho = -0.16 and -0.13).

The spatial correlation matrix of t-value maps (Fig. 7B) agreed with the difference matrix for several pairs but not for others. SampEn and FuzzEn remained strongly correlated spatially (rho = 0.88), and ExSEnt(HD) and HigFracDim showed the strongest negative spatial correlation in the matrix (from rho = -0.62 in Fig. 7A to rho = -0.79 in Fig. 7B). The coupling between the aperiodic exponent and offset was still positive but weaker spatially (rho = 0.68) than at the subject level (rho = 0.86). The negative coupling between aperiodic parameters and SampEn/FuzzEn observed in Fig. 7A (rho = -0.52 to -0.68) was weaker in Fig. 7B (rho = -0.17 to -0.45). Conversely, ExSEnt(HA) and ExSEnt(HDA) showed positive spatial correlations with the aperiodic exponent (rho = 0.40 and 0.71, respectively), which were largely absent in Fig. 7A. Hence, their spatial co-localization with aperiodic effects does not seem to be driven by correlated individual differences in reactivity.

3.3.2. Multiscale measures

Paired permutation tests (2,000 iterations, cluster-based correction over channels and scales, α = 0.05) were conducted on MSE, MFE, and RCMFE separately for the two coarsegraining methods (standard deviation and mean), and on mMSE, whose bandpass scheme does not use a coarse-graining operator.

Using SD coarse-graining (Fig. 8), two measures yielded exclusively negative clusters (EC < EO): multiscale entropy (MSE) produced one cluster spanning scales 5 to 23 across 52 channels (peak: Fpz at scale 12, t = -5.52, Hedges' g = -0.86; Fig. 8A), and multiscale fuzzy entropy (MFE) one cluster spanning scales 6 to 30 across 47 channels (peak: AF3 at scale 13, t = -5.37, Hedges' g = -0.83; Fig. 8B). RCMFE yielded two clusters of opposing sign (Fig. 8C), both spanning all 64 channels: a negative cluster at fine scales (scales 2 to 9; peak: FC3 at scale 2, t = -7.79, Hedges' g = -1.21) and a positive cluster at coarser scales (scales 8 to 30; peak: AF3 at scale 30, t = 7.93, Hedges' g = 1.23). Modified multiscale entropy (mMSE) did not survive FWE correction.

Using mean coarse-graining (Fig. 9), MSE produced one negative cluster spanning scales 2 to 7 across all 64 channels (peak: F2 at scale 2, t = -10.17, Hedges' g = -1.58; Fig. 9A). MFE produced three clusters: a negative cluster at the finest scales (scales 2 to 4, 64 channels; peak: FC3 at scale 2, t = -8.41, Hedges' g = -1.30; Fig. 9B), followed by a positive cluster at intermediate scales (scales 4 to 11, 61 channels; peak: Oz at scale 7, t = 8.63, Hedges' g = 1.34), and a second positive cluster at coarser scales (scales 15 to 25, 39 channels; peak: PO8 at scale 19, t = 5.82, Hedges' g = 0.90). RCMFE yielded three clusters alternating in sign (Fig. 9C): a negative cluster at fine scales (scales 1 to 3, 64 channels; peak: FC1 at scale 2, t = -8.52, Hedges' g = -1.32), a positive cluster at intermediate scales (scales 4 to 13, 64 channels; peak: Iz at scale 6, t = 8.74, Hedges' g = 1.36), and a negative cluster at coarse scales (scales 12 to 30, 48 channels; peak: Iz at scale 28, t = -8.78, Hedges' g = -1.36). Fig. 8. Multiscale entropy differences for three measures ((A) MSE, (B) MFE, (C) RCMFE) between 1-minute eyes-closed (EC) and eyes-open (EO) resting state across 40 participants, using standard deviation as the coarse-graining method.
